meta.title: NZ Politics 2026: What they actually said

facts: Saturday 7 November 2026. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced the date on 21 January 2026.

Runs from Monday 26 October to Friday 6 November 2026. Voting is in person (online voting only for overseas voters). It opens on Labour Day, when fewer voting places will be open; Electoral Commission advice released on 18 October called the 7 November date 'challenging, but manageable' partly for that reason.
Closes at midnight on Sunday 25 October 2026. You cannot enrol or update details after that, and you cannot enrol at a voting place.

More than 90% of eligible voters are enrolled, but only about 67% of 18–24-year-olds (Electoral Commission figures reported by RNZ on 19 October). About 75 locations are open for in-person enrolment this week, or you can enrol online at vote.nz or by post. Same-day enrolment during advance voting and on election day has been abolished.
Opens on Wednesday 21 October 2026 (secondary source: Silvereye's 19 October election brief; the Electoral Commission's own pages blocked our automated check).

The last scheduled Luxon v Hipkins head-to-head, hosted by Stuff and The Post, is on Tuesday 20 October from 7.30pm (RNZ). The Te Tai Tokerau candidates' debate is on Whakaata Māori the same night at 7pm (Te Ao Māori News). The NZ Herald 'Powerbrokers' debate, among leaders of parties likely to be in coalition talks, is on Wednesday 21 October (secondary source: Silvereye).
The official count is due on Friday 27 November 2026. Luxon said formal coalition talks would probably wait for it, and neither he nor Hipkins would promise a deal before Christmas (RNZ, 19 October).
The 54th Parliament was dissolved on 1 October 2026. Ministers stay in office until a new government is formed.
This will not be held with the 2026 election. The government dropped the planned referendum on 18 February 2026 (secondary source: Wikipedia).

context: The current government is the Sixth National Government, formed in November 2023. National leads it with two separate coalition agreements, one with ACT and one with NZ First. Winston Peters was Deputy Prime Minister until 31 May 2025, when David Seymour took over under the agreed rotation.
Seats at dissolution: National 49, ACT 11 and NZ First 8 (government total 68). Labour 34, Greens 15, Te Pāti Māori 4 and two independents (both former Te Pāti Māori MPs). That is 123 seats in total.

Polls in the final month show both major parties well below their 2023 results. The 13 October 1News–Verian poll put National and Labour tied on 28% each (56% together, down from 64.9% at the 2023 election). Neither the current coalition nor a Labour–Green–Te Pāti Māori bloc has a clear majority in these polls, and the Opportunity Party (outside Parliament) is often the kingmaker — on 8% in that poll. Luxon has again ruled out working with Opportunity. A leaked 6–10 October poll by Anacta (Labour's own pollster, reported by The Post on 15 October) also had both majors below 30%: Labour 29%, National 28%, Opportunity 5.4%. The final Post/Freshwater Strategy poll (published 20 October) again had both majors below 30% and Opportunity on 5.4%, just above the threshold. On The Post's seat projection as summarised by the Democracy Project, National, ACT and NZ First would have 59 seats, so Opportunity's seven MPs would decide which side governs.

Leader ratings: in 1News Vote Compass (136,713 participants, 4–11 October, weighted, non-probability), no leader averaged 5 out of 10 for favourability. Hipkins was highest on 4.3, then Swarbrick 4.0, Wong 3.8, Peters 3.7 and Luxon 3.6; Seymour 3.4, Davidson 3.3, Ngarewa-Packer 2.1 and Waititi 1.9 (1News, 17 Oct).

Big issues of 2026: the cost of living (made worse by a fuel-price spike linked to the 2026 Middle East conflict); tax (Labour's capital gains tax, the Greens' wealth taxes, National's 'no new taxes' pledge); two challenges to Luxon's leadership inside National (April and August); the law replacing the RMA, passed in September; Treaty and Waitangi Tribunal policy; immigration; and turmoil inside Te Pāti Māori.
meta.other_parties_note: Te Tai Tokerau Party was founded in May 2026 by Mariameno Kapa-Kingi, the sitting MP for Te Tai Tokerau, after her split from Te Pāti Māori. Its list has two names (Kyla Campbell-Kamariera and Kapa-Kingi). It is not profiled in depth here. It is listed because 1News counts it in the left bloc's seat projections if Kapa-Kingi holds her seat.

parties.name: New Zealand National Party
parties.selection: The leader plus list places 2 to 5 on National's 2026 list (released 8 August 2026): deputy leader Nicola Willis (2), Chris Bishop (3), Simeon Brown (4) and Erica Stanford (5). All four are senior Cabinet ministers.
parties.history: Founded in 1936 from a merger of the United and Reform parties. It is New Zealand's main centre-right party and has led governments under Holland, Holyoake, Muldoon, Bolger/Shipley and Key/English. It won the most votes in 2023 and formed the current government with ACT and NZ First.
parties.ideology: Centre-right. Liberal-conservative, pro-market, and focused on fiscal restraint, law and order, and 'getting the basics right'.
parties.role: Leads the Sixth National Government (since 27 November 2023) under separate coalition agreements with ACT and NZ First. Christopher Luxon is Prime Minister and Nicola Willis is Minister of Finance.
policies: 'No new taxes': on 23 August 2026 Luxon widened the pledge from 'no new taxes on working people' and ruled out a bank tax and a bed (accommodation) tax.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1083119/national-promises-no-new-taxes-if-re-elected
Welfare: Jobseeker changes announced 8 October 2026, including random drug testing ('If you can work, you should').
https://x.com/chrisluxonmp/status/2107949741086765497
Education: NCEA to be replaced by new qualifications (NZCE at Year 12, NZACE at Year 13). Details were confirmed in May 2026.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/595424/government-confirms-ncea-replacement-details
Planning: the Planning Act and Natural Environment Act replacing the RMA passed on 22 September 2026. The full system is intended to be running by 2030.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/260922-chrisbishop
Social media: a bill to ban under-16s from most social media platforms was introduced as a National Party bill in August 2026. ACT and NZ First oppose it (secondary source).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand

Fiscal plan (12 October 2026): tax relief only once the books are back in surplus (not forecast before 2029); a commitment to an independent election policy-costing unit by the 2029 election; $451.8m to extend the school lunch programme to the next election.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1858565/national-hints-at-tax-cuts-after-2029-as-fiscal-plan-released

Superannuation: National confirmed its fiscal plan is its super policy. It still proposes raising the age gradually but sets no date, and commits to cross-party talks within 100 days of a new government.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1860419/politicians-can-t-dance-alone-on-superannuation-nicola-willis
Aid: a plan to cut aid outside the Pacific to fund health spending. Coalition partner NZ First publicly criticised it.
https://x.com/winstonpeters/status/2107229536366850450

Young New Zealanders (13 October 2026): five commitments to legislate or direct in the first 100 days: lower student loan repayment rates for borrowers living in New Zealand, wider access to 5% deposits for first-home buyers, paid parental leave extended from 26 to 30 weeks within three years, a $1500 KiwiSaver 'Baby Boost', and faster visas for partners of New Zealand citizens. National says each is funded to start by 1 July 2027.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/261013-nicolawillis

Plug-in solar (15 October 2026): shops able to sell plug-in solar panels within six months of a re-elected National government, once safety rules being developed with Australia are finished; a Home Energy Fund for rooftop solar, batteries, insulation and heat pumps, repaid through rates; and rooftop solar without a consent.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/261015-simeonbrown-1

Auckland plan (14 October 2026): remove the blanket ban on minimum car-parking requirements and let councils set minimums in suburban areas outside intensification zones, greenfield subdivisions and business parks. Most of the nine-page plan restates enacted or already announced policies.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1887747/national-promises-to-remove-auckland-s-ban-on-minimum-car-parking-rules

Right to silence (18 October 2026, Paul Goldsmith): a new Crimes Act offence of not giving police information when a child under 12 is killed and it is clear one or more adults were present at or before the death, with a maximum of 10 years' prison. National says it would work with legal experts on a narrow exception to the right to silence. Child Matters said the idea needs careful scrutiny.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1978144/national-pledges-to-take-away-right-to-silence-when-a-child-is-murdered

Waikato (19 October 2026, Chris Bishop): if re-elected, start construction of the SH1 Cambridge to Piarere extension of the Waikato Expressway early next year. Most of the release restates projects already under way or announced (Hamilton Southern Links, the Waikato medical school, fast-track approvals for Green Steel and Waihi North).
https://www.national.org.nz/news/20261019-chrisbishop

Social media (19 October 2026): after Labour's announcement, Luxon matched its promise to progress an under-16 social media ban within a new government's first 100 days, saying it had always been his plan to prioritise it next term.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2010803/as-it-happened-election-campaign-19-october

Agriculture manifesto (16 October 2026, AgFest in Greymouth): 19 sets of nationwide rules (national standards) so farmers can do work such as growing vegetables, storing water, managing animal waste, building farm tracks and housing seasonal workers without council consent if they meet the conditions. No timeline was given, and five of the 19 standards repeat earlier announcements. Also up to 70 graduate vets a year supported to work rurally from 2027 (up to $3.4m over four years) and $16m over four years for wild deer, goat and pest control from the international visitor levy.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1952424/national-promises-fewer-council-approvals-for-farms
events: April 2026: after media reports of caucus discontent, Luxon called a confidence vote on his own leadership and won it (21 April). A reshuffle earlier that month moved the campaign-chair role from Chris Bishop to Simeon Brown.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/592984/prime-minister-christopher-luxon-survives-confidence-vote
August 2026: Chris Penk challenged Luxon. Luxon survived a second confidence vote on 12 August and stripped Penk of his portfolios. Penk later withdrew as a candidate.
https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/08/12/pm-wins-leadership-vote-after-challenge-fails-penk-wont-seek-re-election/
September 2026: the Advertising Standards Authority partly upheld a complaint that a National attack ad on Labour's capital gains tax was misleading.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1311337/asa-partly-upholds-complaint-against-misleading-national-attack-ad
Budget 2026 (28 May) was billed as restrained. Willis said she had not convinced coalition partners to raise the NZ Super age.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/596665/just-need-to-vote-for-it-nicola-willis-ends-budget-speech-with-call-to-arms-for-supporters
Luxon has ruled out working with the Opportunity Party, and has called strategic vote-splitting 'insanely stupid'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1749693/rnz-reid-research-poll-national-crashes-greens-surge-opportunity-kingmaker

13 October 2026: after a 1News–Verian poll tied National and Labour on 28% with Opportunity on 8%, Luxon again ruled out working with Opportunity and a grand coalition, and said it would be a 'very, very tight election'.
https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/13/poll-hipkins-and-luxon-now-neck-and-neck-opportunity-on-track-for-10-mps/

14 October 2026, NZ Herald leaders' debate: Luxon again ruled out Opportunity. He said the minimum wage would rise with inflation ('that's what we've more or less been doing'), though RNZ notes it rose by less than inflation in each of the past three years, and said Foodstuffs would be split 'for sure', which the moderator noted depends on the Commerce Commission.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1912632/debate-doubts-does-anyone-believe-the-two-chrises

14 October 2026: Winston Peters' office called National's claim that foreign aid had risen 26% since 2021 'incorrect', saying the inflation-adjusted rise was about 10%. National stands by its unadjusted figure.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1884968/national-s-claim-foreign-aid-increased-by-26-percent-incorrect-winston-peters-says

15 October 2026: Health Minister Simeon Brown rejected reports that cancer treatment at Starship children's hospital had been suspended because of nursing shortages, saying no child had missed out on care and that the eight vacant specialist nursing roles had been filled or were being recruited. A mother told RNZ her toddler's treatment had been delayed.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/1942123/mother-heartbroken-toddler-s-cancer-treatment-delayed-by-starship-hospital-staff-shortages
14 October 2026: justice spokesperson Paul Goldsmith accused the Greens and Te Pāti Māori of 'prioritising' gangs over victims after their candidates attended a Mongrel Mob election hui.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1896798/greens-unapologetic-at-mongrel-mob-meeting-as-national-cries-foul

17 October 2026: RNZ checked Luxon's August claim that the government had 'certainly strengthened healthcare'. Nationally, 76.3% of emergency department patients were seen within six hours (March–June 2026), five points better than Labour's last figures in 2023, but about half of hospitals went backwards year on year and the figures predate this winter's flu outbreak. Simeon Brown said the results also showed where more work and investment were needed.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/1963704/christopher-luxon-says-his-government-has-certainly-strengthened-healthcare-has-it-really

18 October 2026: RNZ reported that Luxon chose 7 November although the Electoral Commission called it 'challenging, but manageable' (advance voting starts on Labour Day) and saw 17 October and 21 November as more feasible. Labour accused him of 'knowingly limiting turnout'. Luxon said 'We picked this date', and on 19 October laughed off claims of voter suppression, saying more people are enrolled now than at this stage of the last election.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1974290/prime-minister-passed-over-easier-election-dates-advice-reveals

19 October 2026: lawyers criticised National's right-to-silence policy. Defence lawyer Marie Dyhrberg KC said it 'flies in the face of justice' and reverses the burden of proof; retired law professor Bill Hodge said it would change police interviews in a way he called 'dangerous', though he did not feel as strongly.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2009985/national-s-pledge-to-remove-right-to-silence-when-a-child-is-murdered-flies-in-face-of-justice-lawyers-say

19 October 2026: Luxon denied the health system was in crisis after Starship treatment delays and warnings from Wairau Hospital's emergency department, saying 'we are making progress' and pointing to emergency-department waiting times. Hipkins then challenged him to a debate on health; RNZ said it had approached National for comment.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2023715/chris-hipkins-challenges-christopher-luxon-to-debate-on-health

19 October 2026: at the Cambridge to Piarere Expressway site Luxon challenged NZTA chief executive Brett Gliddon to finish the $1.8b, five-year project in 18 months ('go 24/7'). Gliddon called that 'a bit ambitious'. Luxon later called it 'a coaching conversation', not criticism.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/2030661/prime-minister-s-coaching-conversation-with-nzta-boss-over-road-project-delivery

19 October 2026: after Oriini Kaipara's comments about the Mongrel Mob, Luxon said gangs 'peddle misery and death and suffering', called the Greens and Te Pāti Māori MPs who visited the gang pad 'muppets', and urged centrist Labour voters to party-vote National. At a Hamilton rally he told supporters the Mongrel Mob would be part of a Labour-led coalition.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2010803/as-it-happened-election-campaign-19-october

17 October 2026: asked again about Opportunity, Luxon repeated that he had ruled it out and said he would not prefer opposition: 'we're going to win'. At Hobsonville's Catalina Bay market a breast cancer volunteer told him she disagreed with National's plan to fund more medicines by cutting foreign aid; Luxon said the plan takes 10% off the aid budget.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1967290/as-it-happened-election-campaign-17-october

parties.name: New Zealand Labour Party
parties.selection: The leader plus list places 2 to 5 on Labour's list (released 8 June 2026): deputy leader Carmel Sepuloni, finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds, Willie Jackson and Megan Woods.
parties.history: Founded in 1916 and New Zealand's oldest current party. It built the welfare state under Savage (1935) and has led governments under Fraser, Nash, Kirk, Lange, Clark and Ardern/Hipkins. It lost power in 2023 after two terms.
parties.role: Official Opposition. Chris Hipkins (Prime Minister January to November 2023) is leader and is seeking to form a government with the Greens and, potentially, Te Pāti Māori and/or Opportunity.
policies: A capital gains tax on property only (28%, excluding the family home and farms, from July 2027) to fund three free GP visits a year for everyone through a 'Medicard'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/577021/labour-to-campaign-on-narrow-capital-gains-tax-no-wealth-tax
An 'NZ Future Fund' modelled on Singapore's Temasek, announced October 2025 (secondary source).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party
A 10% write-off of eligible student loan balances, announced at the 27 September campaign launch.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1615271/it-made-me-so-angry-hipkins-targets-cost-of-living-at-labour-campaign-launch
A $160m 'SolarSaver' package with subsidies and loans for rooftop and plug-in solar.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/685297/labour-promises-subsidies-new-loan-schemes-for-installing-solar

Cheaper school uniforms (limits on compulsory branded items and generic alternatives allowed), announced 12 October, alongside locally made school lunches from Term 1 2028 and restoring 43 cancelled rural school bus routes 'where possible'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1857589/labour-plans-to-cut-school-uniform-costs-and-allow-affordable-generic-options

Local government (15 October 2026, LGNZ conference): Hipkins said Labour would expand its proposed ratepayer assistance scheme to cover rates and development contributions, and that 'everything should be on the table' for council funding, including visitor levies.
https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/15/political-punching-bag-hipkins-says-councils-made-scapegoats/

Kids Off Screens (18 October 2026): $7m a year for children's sport and after-school activities ($3m to keep the Active Me – Kia Tū grants of up to $300 a year, and $4m through Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa for community groups); updated screen-use guidance for early childhood and schools, with school boards required to set screen-use policies; keep the school phone ban.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1985304/labour-pledges-7-million-to-get-kids-off-screens-and-back-to-being-kids

Online safety (19 October 2026, Hipkins and Reuben Davidson): get the under-16 social media ban bill to select committee within the first 100 days; a 'Digital Duty of Care' law within the first year making platforms identify and fix risks (bullying, self-harm content, deepfakes, 'nudify' apps); an independent online regulator able to fine companies; and a choice between algorithm-driven and following-only feeds. (RNZ corrected an earlier report that Labour would implement the ban within 100 days.) Peters called it 'a naive solution to a genuine issue'.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2015458/labour-pledges-social-media-ban-for-under-16s
Visa-waiver travel for Pacific Islands Forum citizens.
https://asiapacificreport.nz/2026/09/17/labour-promises-visa-free-travel-for-pacific-as-overstayer-rates-rise/

Economic plan (14 October 2026): redirect up to $50m a year of the government's NZ Super Fund contribution into the Elevate venture capital fund; make big businesses pay small suppliers within 15 days; immediate write-off of new tools and equipment up to $10,000; raise the GST threshold to $80,000; back 30,000 apprentices with a $1000 tools grant; surplus in 2028/29, restore the Reserve Bank's dual mandate and set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1896823/labour-unveils-economic-plan-pledges-up-to-50m-a-year-for-venture-capital-fund
events: Reversal on capital gains tax: in July 2023 Hipkins ruled out a CGT 'End of story'. In October 2025 Labour adopted a property CGT.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/493596/hipkins-rules-out-capital-gains-tax-wealth-tax-if-labour-re-elected
National and Labour co-sponsored modern slavery legislation (January 2026), over ACT's opposition. Labour also backed the NZ–India FTA, which NZ First opposed (secondary source).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand
Labour's costings were attacked by National ('the least credible fiscal plan… in living memory'). Labour says its plan is fully costed.
https://www.national.org.nz/news/261004-nicolawillis
22 September 2026: list-only candidate Warrick Cleine withdrew after controversy over the fact that he does not live in New Zealand (secondary source).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_lists_in_the_2026_New_Zealand_general_election
Labour is contesting the Māori seats hard against Te Pāti Māori, and has criticised TPM's candidate-vote-only strategy.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/1052259/te-pati-maori-warned-election-strategy-could-put-maori-seats-at-risk

14 October 2026, NZ Herald leaders' debate: Hipkins ruled out giving law-and-order portfolios to any Green or Te Pāti Māori MP after their candidates were photographed with Mongrel Mob members, and said Chlöe Swarbrick could never be Treasurer (RNZ's wording). In a quick-fire round he put a lower voting age, a rainbow affairs ministry and compulsory te reo 'on the table', and ruled out binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations and a higher corporate tax.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1916478/chris-hipkins-leaders-debate-strategy-let-luxon-talk-himself-into-trouble

15 October 2026: Hipkins called the Green and Te Pāti Māori candidates' Mongrel Mob photos 'really, really ill considered' and said any potential minister of his who posed with gang members 'wouldn't be a member of the cabinet'. Willie Jackson said the meeting was not a good strategic move. Davidson stood by it.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1923070/greens-marama-davidson-doubles-down-amid-outrage-over-gang-visit
15 October 2026: at a Kelston rally Hipkins used Labour's new attack line that Luxon has left people $6000 worse off (Labour's own calculation, which it has also published as an online calculator).
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1940271/labour-supporters-told-to-harness-hope-and-rage-national-voters-fear-handout-society

14 October 2026, ASB finance debate: Edmonds and Willis clashed over Investment Boost, which Labour would replace with a policy targeting small businesses. Both back cross-party talks on superannuation.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1905390/what-we-learnt-from-a-rough-and-tumble-finance-debate

15 October 2026, LGNZ conference in Rotorua: Hipkins said councils had been left 'in limbo' by the government's paused Head Start amalgamation programme. He said Labour would keep pursuing local government reform but with more community input and without 'arbitrary deadlines', and voiced reservations about abolishing regional councils. Local Government Minister Simon Watts ruled out reimbursing councils for their Head Start costs.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/1950872/you-made-us-do-it-frustrated-councils-clash-with-minister-over-reform-costs

18 October 2026, TVNZ Q+A: Hipkins called the end of same-day enrolment 'reckless' and said the Electoral Commission had 'absolutely not' done enough to warn voters, but said Labour would accept the election result. He said he wanted to look at moving the Social Investment Agency into the Prime Minister's department, and was 'very open' to discussing legislated minimum safe staffing levels in hospitals.
https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/18/hipkins-worried-about-very-angry-voters-over-govts-enrolment-changes/

19 October 2026: Hipkins rejected Oriini Kaipara's promise to 'restore mana' to Mongrel Mob members, calling gangs 'a scourge on society', and said Labour would not support changes to the gang patch ban. Health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall said Labour would end any hiring freeze and prioritise staffing oncology at Starship.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2018789/te-pati-maori-s-oriini-kaipara-on-gangs-i-see-whanau

19 October 2026: Hipkins challenged Luxon to a debate on health in a social media video, saying the health system was 'in crisis'. On coalition timing he would not promise a deal before Christmas: 'If you want a good, decisive outcome, vote for one. Vote Labour.'
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/2023715/chris-hipkins-challenges-christopher-luxon-to-debate-on-health

17 October 2026: asked about campaign chair Kieran McAnulty saying he would rather work with Opportunity than Te Pāti Māori, Hipkins said those were 'conversations for after the election' and that, for now, a vote for Opportunity risked re-electing the current government. At a Papatoetoe meeting of ethnic community leaders he said a minister of his making comments like those of Winston Peters and Shane Jones would be sacked, and that Labour would not fund any gang programmes in government.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1967290/as-it-happened-election-campaign-17-october

parties.name: Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand
parties.selection: Both co-leaders plus the next four places on the final members-ranked list (released 22 April 2026): Teanau Tuiono (3), Tamatha Paul (4), Julie Anne Genter (5) and Lan Pham (6).
parties.history: Formed in 1990, with roots in the Values Party (1972). It was part of the Alliance until 1997 and has had MPs in its own right since 1999. It was in a cooperation agreement with Labour from 2017 to 2023. Chlöe Swarbrick became female co-leader in March 2024, alongside Marama Davidson.
parties.ideology: Left. Environmentalist, with a focus on social and economic justice and Te Tiriti.
parties.role: Opposition. The Greens have said 'very clearly' they want to form a government with Labour. Their best-ever polls came in late September and early October 2026 (up to 16% in 1News–Verian); the 13 October Verian poll had them on 15%.
policies: A tax package with a wealth tax, an inheritance tax and higher corporate tax, paired with income-tax cuts the party says would benefit 96% of people.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/609649/greens-propose-wealth-corporate-and-inheritance-taxes-to-fund-income-tax-changes
Free public transport for children and students and a $2 adult fare. A $4b plan to restore intercity passenger rail.
https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/04/greens-pledge-free-buses-trains-for-kids-students-2-adult-fare-cap/
A National Electrification Plan announced during the 2026 fuel crisis.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/592794/green-party-issues-human-catastrophe-warning-in-state-of-the-planet-address

Regulating artificial intelligence (12 October): no fully automated decisions in public services that make a substantive difference to people's lives, explicit consent standards for AI training data, and environmental impact assessments for hyperscale data centres.
